lessons.title: Housing design and siting
lessons.html:
Housing design and siting

Poultry houses are long-term investments that determine how well the manager can control the birds' environment and biosecurity. Design decisions affect performance, energy costs and welfare for decades.

Siting

  • Biosecurity: distance from other poultry farms, public roads and wild bird areas such as dams and wetlands.
  • Orientation: in South Africa, open-sided houses are usually oriented east-west to reduce direct sun on the side walls.
  • Drainage: elevated, well-drained sites; rainwater must not run into houses.
  • Services: reliable electricity, water supply and road access for feed trucks and bird transport.
  • Neighbours and law: zoning, environmental authorisations where required, and odour and fly impacts on neighbours.
  • Site layout: clean and dirty zones; a single controlled entrance; houses spaced for ventilation and fire safety.

House types

TypeFeaturesConsiderations
Open-sided (curtain)Natural ventilation with adjustable curtainsLower capital and energy cost; less control in extreme weather
Closed, environment-controlledInsulated, mechanical ventilation, evaporative cooling, controllersHigh capital and electricity dependence; best performance and control
Free-range housesHouse plus outdoor range and pop holesBiosecurity risk from wild birds; range management
Layer cage or aviary systemsMulti-tier systems with egg belts and manure beltsHigh density; buyer and welfare standards are changing

Construction features

Insulated roofs and walls reduce heat gain and loss. Concrete floors are easier to clean and disinfect. Bird-proof netting and sealed gaps keep out wild birds and rodents. Smooth, washable surfaces support cleaning. Every house should have a clean anteroom with a foot bath, hand wash and clothing change area.

lessons.title: Environmental control equipment
lessons.html:
Environmental control equipment

Ventilation

  • Minimum ventilation: timer-controlled fans and inlets give fresh air in cold weather without chilling birds.
  • Transitional ventilation: more fans and inlets as temperature rises.
  • Tunnel ventilation: large fans at one end pull air along the house at speed to create wind chill in hot weather.
  • Inlets: must direct air correctly; poorly adjusted inlets cause draughts or dead spots.

Cooling

Evaporative cooling pads at the air inlet cool air by evaporating water; foggers or misters are an alternative. Pads need clean water, regular cleaning and inspection, and control so that humidity does not become too high.

Heating

Brooding uses gas heaters, radiant brooders, coal or wood stoves, or underfloor heating. Heaters must be serviced, positioned so chicks can move to their comfort zone, and vented to prevent carbon monoxide build-up. Gas installations must comply with safety requirements and be checked for leaks.

Lighting

Lighting systems with dimmers and timers deliver the programme required. LED lighting is energy-efficient. Light should be evenly distributed; dark corners lead to floor eggs in layers or poor feeding in broilers.

Controllers and alarms

Environment controllers integrate temperature, humidity, sometimes ammonia or CO2 sensors, and run fans, inlets, heaters and cooling. Alarms must alert staff to high or low temperatures and power failures, by siren and phone. Test alarms regularly.

Standby power

Load shedding makes standby generators essential. Generators must be sized for the full load, start automatically, be serviced and test-run under load regularly, with fuel reserves for extended outages. Keep a written procedure for generator failure.

lessons.title: Feeding, watering and egg equipment, and maintenance
lessons.html:
Feeding, watering and egg equipment, and maintenance

Feeding systems

Feed is delivered in bulk to silos and moved by augers to pan feeders or chain feeders in the house. Chicks start on paper or trays with feed for easy access. Key points:

  • Enough feeder space per bird as the management guide specifies.
  • Feeder height adjusted to the birds' back height as they grow.
  • Feed level in pans adjusted to reduce wastage.
  • Silos kept sealed and clean to prevent moulds and pests; clean out between flocks.
  • Feed weighing systems or silo load cells help monitor intake.

Watering systems

Nipple drinker lines with drip cups are standard in modern houses; bell drinkers are used in some systems. Manage line height and pressure for bird age. Water meters per house are essential. Medication dosers (proportioners) allow vaccines and treatments to be given through water - calibrate and clean them. Clean and sanitise lines between flocks and use water sanitation during the flock as the vet advises.

Egg handling equipment

In layer and breeder houses, nest boxes or cage systems, egg belts, collection tables, graders and packers handle eggs. Equipment must be adjusted to reduce cracks, cleaned to prevent contamination, and maintained to avoid downtime. Egg rooms need temperature control. Hatching eggs need careful handling and storage.

Maintenance management

TypeExamples
Daily checksDrinker leaks, feeder operation, fan running, alarms, generator status
Between-flock maintenanceFan belts and shutters, inlet adjustments, pad cleaning, line flushing, repairs
Planned servicingGenerators, heaters, controllers, augers, graders
CalibrationSensors, scales, water meters, dosers

Keep a maintenance register per house. Plan major work for the clean-out period. Ensure guards are in place on augers, fans and belts, and that lock-out procedures are followed during repairs, as required by the OHS Act 85 of 1993.

Key points

  • Site houses for biosecurity, drainage, services and orientation.
  • Closed houses give the best control but depend on electricity.
  • Match ventilation mode to weather and bird age; keep inlets correctly adjusted.
  • Test alarms and run generators under load regularly.
  • Maintain equipment daily, between flocks and on a service schedule.
